Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies Latest York Symposium

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1410 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.
  • Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions.
  • “I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 19:21 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.

Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions. Meanwhile, AI is changing the threat landscape, giving less sophisticated attackers access to capabilities that once required considerably greater resources, according to John Scimone, president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc.

“I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE. “Stated another way, the least sophisticated attack tomorrow is more sophisticated than the world will have ever seen a year ago.”.

Scimone spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante during the Dell Technologies Upcoming York Symposium, part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exclusive coverage on theCUBE. Across the event, Dell executives and cloud infrastructure providers examined the economics of enterprise AI, the operational challenges of scaling infrastructure and the decisions shaping AI adoption.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Scimone:.

Here are three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies Fresh York Symposium:.

Dell has spent nearly two years running fully autonomous agents internally, capturing institutional knowledge in machine-readable skill files that guide their behavior. The effort is part of a broader reorganization of work around AI agents, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

It has been revealed that “It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” he stated during the event. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these new forms that really capture what you know and do differently than your competitors.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Roese:.

Sources indicate that the financial side of AI operational readiness presents a different challenge. As enterprises scale their deployments, finance teams are establishing dedicated budget lines for token consumption and evaluating which workloads can run more economically on-premises. Repetitive financial processes, for example, can use open-weight models to convert variable token expenses into more predictable fixed costs, according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell.

Sources indicate that “It’s not necessarily about the amount and the cost of a token,” he told theCUBE. “It’s about the tokens you use. Can you be efficient with them? If you are, you’re going to see great outcomes.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Kennedy:.

Sources indicate that the growth of AI inference is changing how enterprises distribute workloads across cloud environments, data centers and edge devices. Dell’s expanded agentic AI portfolio reflects that shift, with solutions spanning desktop systems and data center infrastructure. Organizations are evaluating where to run models based on performance, data control and cost, according to Kyle Dufresne, senior vice president of sales at Dell.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re seeing the business owners saying, ‘Oh my gosh, these costs are getting really high for inferencing. How do we reduce those costs without curbing innovation?’” he noted during the event. “We’re finding it’s happening across that continuum but more and more right out at the far edge.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Kyle Dufresne:.

Infrastructure availability presents another challenge. Demand for AI servers has strained supplies of components ranging from memory and processors to rack-level cooling, networking and power equipment, according to David Schmoock, senior vice president of global revenue operations at Dell.

Sources indicate that “We didn’t do that collaborative planning, and now your project may have been delayed 60, 90, 120 days, which has both the cost impact and a business impact,” he told theCUBE. “I would say bring us in earlier. Allow us to do that collaboration with you. I think, at the end of the day, you get the most optimal outcome.”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Schmoock:.

Recent findings suggest that AI operational readiness is also becoming a consideration for smaller businesses that need access to GPU computing without the resources of large enterprises. Comet Cloud Inc. is targeting this underserved market, where access to AI infrastructure can be constrained by purchasing commitments and provider priorities, according to Thomas Kato, founder and chief executive officer of Comet Cloud.

“You go to [Amazon Web Services] now; they want a multiyear contract from you. They’re picking who they’re taking,” he said during the event. “To the small and medium businesses, they’re not even coming up on that scope at all to be able to have that AI. Really, that’s our focus.”.

Comet Cloud is developing an alternative approach aimed at giving smaller organizations greater control over their computing environments, Kato noted.

“What we do is we put together clusters, and we’re giving clusters to a whole organization. All their information, all their security, everything is within that cluster. There’s no one else tied or connected to it,” he told theCUBE.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Thomas Kato:.

Sources indicate that alpha Compute Corp. is also building its neocloud infrastructure around data sovereignty and confidential computing requirements. The company’s sovereign-by-design approach is intended to help customers maintain control over sensitive workloads and meet data residency obligations, including those associated with European regulations, according to Tom Richer, executive vice president of Alpha Compute.

“We start with the hardware. Think of a stack. All the way down to the chip level, we are creating enclaves,” he told theCUBE. “We’re a Dell partner, so we use Dell technology as well as Intel technology.”.

Recent findings suggest that keeping GPU infrastructure operational presents a different challenge for neocloud providers. Alpha Compute provides integrated infrastructure support and ongoing managed services to address those demands, Richer noted.

“You can cobble together a lot of different providers, but then when stuff goes wrong, the finger-pointing starts,” he said during the event. “You just want that integrated solution provider who can ensure success, help you with all of the build-out, then all of the … managed services to keep it going healthy and to keep everything performing in line with [service-level agreements].”.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Tom Richer:.

Breaking: Ripple-Backed Evernorth Cuts XRP Holdings by 60%

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (288 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Ripple-backed XRP treasury firm Evernorth has suffered substantial losses on its XRP ventures amid the persistent volatility facing the broad crypto market since the third quarter of 2026.
  • Sources indicate that the firm has reported a massive write-down of its XRP holdings for Q3 2026 in a recent filing with the U.S.
  • On Tuesday, November 17, Evernorth reported a substantial decline in the value of its XRP holdings after the firm wrote down over $505 million in its latest financial filing with the SEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Ripple-backed XRP treasury firm Evernorth has suffered substantial losses on its XRP ventures amid the persistent volatility facing the broad crypto market since the third quarter of 2026.

Sources indicate that the firm has reported a massive write-down of its XRP holdings for Q3 2026 in a recent filing with the U.S. SEC, drawing attention from the broader crypto community.

On Tuesday, November 17, Evernorth reported a substantial decline in the value of its XRP holdings after the firm wrote down over $505 million in its latest financial filing with the SEC.

Notably, Evernorth issued a Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, disclosing that it holds around 346 million XRP, now valued at about $342 million.

This has drawn attention across the XRP community and sparked discussions about the growing impact of persistent volatility on investors’ funds, as Evernorth’s XRP report marks a sharp drop from its initial valuation of $847 million.

Apparently, the firm reported that the tokens are now valued at about 40 cents per dollar of their initial worth. This means that the leading XRP treasury firm has reduced the value of its XRP holdings by nearly 60%.

It is important to note that the massive drop in the value of Evernorth’s XRP holdings does not mean that the firm has sold off its XRP. Rather, it marks a write-down in its previously listed XRP value.

The move may have been influenced by the persistent market drawdown, especially after XRP lost support at the key $1 level, closing steadily around $0.90 over the past few days.

Furthermore, Evernorth has specified that it has no intention of reversing the write-downs, even if the price of XRP later recovers.

I Didn’t Have a TV At Home — So I Built a Computer At Age 13 to Compensate. Now My Startup Is On Track to Unlock $1 Billion in Value.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this as-told-to story is based on a conversation with R.C.
  • In his mid-20s, he co-founded CompIQ, a startup focused on helping employers make compensation decisions.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve always been someone who has had high self-agency, a huge amount of self-trust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this as-told-to story is based on a conversation with R.C. Willenbrock, founder of AIVC, an AI firm that rebuilds operational and service-focused businesses with AI. Willenbrock, 35, describes himself as the “tech rebel” of his family because both of his parents and his brother had long careers in finance. He started off in finance but ended up taking a different path deeper into computer science and AI.

In his mid-20s, he co-founded CompIQ, a startup focused on helping employers make compensation decisions. He served as its chief product officer until AI recruitment startup Stella.ai acquired it in 2018. Willenbrock began building AIVC, short for AI Value Creation, in October 2025 and is still working at the startup as a builder. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

According to recent reports, I’ve always been someone who has had high self-agency, a huge amount of self-trust. I grew up in Denver and somehow found myself many years later in New York City.

At an early age, you could call me the tech rebel in the family. The rebel in me came out early. We didn’t have TVs growing up in our household, so when it came time to try and figure out how to get a TV in the bedroom, I just built a computer with TV on it. I was 13 years old.

Early on, I was motivated by achievement and success, and I understood those pretty conventionally. I went to Dartmouth, then Morgan Stanley, then into growth equity. Those were paths I understood and respected.

Sources indicate that in growth equity, I was basically a glorified cold-caller, talking to founders about businesses they had built. That opened up my sense of what a career could look like. I was curious about the problems they were solving, and I wanted a more direct hand in the outcome.

Over time, that took me into building companies, product development and work that was harder to explain with one job title.

The connecting thread was wanting to solve problems and have a direct hand in the outcome. It took time to stop measuring my choices against what looked like a prestigious career and start trusting what genuinely motivated me.

My first business was Stickworks (started in middle school), stringing lacrosse sticks for people in the neighborhood and on my brother’s teams. I hadn’t even started playing lacrosse myself; I just loved stringing the sticks. I was much less interested in collecting the money, which turned out to be a fairly crucial part of running a business.

Sources indicate that compIQ, the compensation benchmarking and pay-equity business I started later, taught me something harder. I put all my savings into it and made a lot of mistakes early on, including hiring mistakes. Eventually, the business was on a strong trajectory, and I had brilliant people on the team.

Recent findings suggest that I never intended to start AIVC. It grew out of a persistent problem that I couldn’t stop working on. Through my work with companies and private equity firms, I kept seeing the same gap. People could identify opportunities for AI, but turning those opportunities into a better business required someone to bring together technology, people, operating decisions and responsibility for the result. That work kept falling between organizations.

My view is that AI is making more of the analytical and financial-engineering work in investing easier to reproduce. The hard part is understanding how much value you can create in a particular business and then actually creating it. That was the work I wanted to pursue.

Our first clients came in 2025 through relationships I had built over years. A few private equity firms gave us access to their portfolio companies, and we also had clients outside that network. They knew me and trusted me to deliver.

Recent findings suggest that that history mattered. We had multiple paying clients before AIVC formally launched in April 2026. From the beginning, I wanted our commercial approach tied to outcomes, because I had seen companies pay a lot for work without getting the result they needed. The proposition was that we would put the right people on the problem and take responsibility for making the business better.

Revenue for AIVC’s first year is in the eight figures.

Sources indicate that but the number we run the company on is the value we create for clients, because we only earn when they do. We align our incentives with the client — because ultimately our goal is to create value (it’s in our name: AI Value Creation). We get paid when our clients win, so our revenue trails the value we create, sometimes by a lot.

According to recent reports, this year we will have created more than $1 billion in enterprise value across our engagements. Eighty percent of the quantified potential is tied to revenue or capacity-led growth, not cost-cutting. This is extremely vital to us because most of the AI story revolves around cost-cutting and human displacement. We want to unlock growth by unlocking human capacity — making humans more human.

Industry observers note that be honest about the support that makes taking a risk possible. I’ve taken some massive risks, and I haven’t always judged them correctly.

According to recent reports, my parents were the backbone that allowed me to take them. They invested time, effort, money and confidence in me. I knew it was okay if I failed.

Recent findings suggest that they’ve worked together for almost 40 years and built their wealth management business within a larger organization. My career has looked very different, but their backing has been fundamental to it. I also have a close group of friends who have been there through the uncertainty.

That’s part of what I want AIVC to provide for other people. There are brilliant people who want to build something and own a meaningful part of the outcome, but making that move can mean taking on more risk than they can carry alone. I want us to provide capital, teammates, resources and someone who will stand behind them when the first attempt doesn’t work.

Industry observers note that get specific about what you’re good at and what you’re bad at. That affects who you hire, what you delegate and where you spend your own time. If you can’t name your weaknesses, it’s easy to build a team of people like you and leave the same gaps uncovered.

Then be someone those people can rely on. You don’t have to be the smartest person in the room. You do have to do the small things well, including the work you don’t feel like doing, and keep improving when things are going well enough that you could get comfortable.

According to recent reports, before taking a big risk, work through the best outcome, the most likely outcome and the worst outcome — and what you would actually do in each. Taking a risk and understanding it should go together.

Talent gets you noticed, and habits get you where you’re going. Do the small, boring things right every day, the ones nobody claps for, because they compound. Most founders overestimate what one big move can do and underestimate what 1,000 small ones will do.

This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with R.C. Willenbrock, founder of AIVC, an AI firm that rebuilds operational and service-focused businesses with AI. Willenbrock, 35, describes himself as the “tech rebel” of his family because both of his parents and his brother had long careers in finance. He started off in finance but ended up taking a different path deeper into computer science and AI.

Industry observers note that in his mid-20s, he co-founded CompIQ, a startup focused on helping employers make compensation decisions. He served as its chief product officer until AI recruitment startup Stella.ai acquired it in 2018. Willenbrock began building AIVC, short for AI Value Creation, in October 2025 and is still working at the startup as a builder. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

#76407. Industry News: Inside the race to put computers in the human brain

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2054 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Inside the race to put computers in the human brain

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A robotic arm drills a circle into the patient’s skull, then places a quarter-size device onto the brain tissue.
  • That’s the promise of the N1 implant made by Neuralink, the brain-computer interface (BCI) tech giant owned by Elon Musk.
  • In a recent development, although no brain implants are on the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A robotic arm drills a circle into the patient’s skull, then places a quarter-size device onto the brain tissue. Dangling from it are 64 wires, each thinner than a human hair. Electrodes along the wires pick up electrical signals from neurons in the brain, and the implant transmits that data to a phone or tablet. The patient can text friends, post on social media, and even play video games—all without lifting a finger.

That’s the promise of the N1 implant made by Neuralink, the brain-computer interface (BCI) tech giant owned by Elon Musk. Neuralink has made science fiction a reality for the approximately 26 people using the device today in the product’s testing phase. All have severe disabilities, but Musk founded the company in 2016 with the goal of far broader adoption. In 2017 he argued that humans will need to connect our brains to technology to keep up with artificial intelligence and avoid “being left behind and being effectively useless, or like a pet.” By 2025, Neuralink was valued at roughly $9.7 billion.

In a recent development, although no brain implants are on the U.S. market yet, the first one that becomes available will be a watershed moment—for the tech sector, for society, arguably for humanity—setting off what those in the industry expect to be a decades-long process to merge our minds with machines. BCIs stand to become increasingly interwoven in our everyday lives, spawning new businesses and demanding new norms to govern their use.

Recent findings suggest that at stake for the companies pioneering these devices is a potentially massive market, both for the devices and the vast troves of data they’ll gather. For the rest of us, the question is what, if anything, we gain by giving corporations access to the sanctity of our thoughts—to profit off and perhaps even shape.

In a recent development, “What you’re thinking and feeling is your last space of true privacy. It’s the most fundamental aspect of what it means to be human,” notes Nita Farahany, a professor at Duke University who authored a book on defending the freedom of thought in an era of brain implants. “We are rapidly heading toward a world of brain transparency, in which scientists, doctors, governments, and companies may peer into our brains and minds at will. Companies [could] know what products we want before we do.”.

It has been revealed that neuralink is one in a growing field of U.S. companies developing BCIs, each sprinting to win Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for public sale. Those include Paradromics, which is focused on restoring speech, and Precision Neuroscience, which is pursuing a brain interface for patients with paralysis.

“It is definitely a race,” says Chad Bouton, CEO of the BCI organization Neuvotion, which makes a commercially available, AI-guided wearable that can help restore movement in stroke and spinal cord injury patients. “I think in the next three or four years we might see an FDA clearance.”.

Neuralink, with $1.3 billion in funding, more than double the next-best-funded brain implant company, might seem a shoo-in to come out ahead, but a rival BCI company, called Synchron, is neck and neck in the FDA process. Synchron’s device—which is less invasive and doesn’t require a skull-breaking craniotomy—may well be first to market.

According to recent reports, thomas Oxley, founder and CEO of Synchron, revealed to Fortune that his organization has implanted its Stentrode device in 15 people, adding five more since last year. In that same period, Neuralink has gone from seven patients to 26. “They’re going fast,” said Oxley, who is himself a neurosurgeon.

Sources indicate that the race had been underway for years before AI became a household term with the debut of ChatGPT in 2022. But rapidly advancing AI stands to dramatically enhance the power of brain implants by allowing them to better decipher our thoughts and intentions.

One day, AI-enhanced BCIs could enable us to control humanoid robots or AI agents on our behalf, taking instructions directly from our thoughts, indicates Matt Angle, CEO of Paradromics. As the research goes “cognitively upstream from language,” he says, the implants could know our desires before we are even aware of them. If a human is hungry, for example, “then the BCI would already understand what we are hungry for, and it would deduce the next reasonable thing,” Angle mentioned—perhaps ordering food on a delivery app. “It won’t be mainstream right away,” he explained, but “it’ll come sooner than a lot of people are expecting.”.

For workers, brain implants could usher in a upcoming wave of employee surveillance in the name of productivity. Connecting a BCI to a work computer could help us type and navigate our computers faster, while also recording biological signals that reveal whether we are focused on work, or letting our minds wander. Employers could even nudge us back to work if BCIs develop two-way communication, Farahany writes in her book. She suspects punitive brain surveillance is unlikely to be tolerated by the public—but even today we accept new forms of workplace tracking, from how many times a day we badge-in to the office to transcriptions of what we say in meetings and monitoring of which applications we open on our computer.

“What you’re thinking and feeling is your last space of true privacy.”.

Some argue that the “cyborgization” of humanity has already begun, even if the devices and algorithms that we’re joined with are external to the body. In a 2017 blog post titled “The Merge,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote, “Our phones control us and tell us what to do and when; social media feeds determine how we feel; search engines decide what we think.” By 2025, an OpenAI analysis of 1.5 million ChatGPT conversations found that roughly three-quarters concerned practical guidance, information seeking, or writing—suggesting that people are increasingly turning to AI to help decide what to do and what to say.

It has been revealed that altman cofounded the BCI manufacturer Merge Labs in 2025, and in early 2026, OpenAI invested in it. The company’s goal is to create a more “seamless” relationship with AI—presumably ChatGPT, or one of the models behind it. A Merge Labs spokesperson wasn’t ready to reveal its product yet in our conversation, but expects to have more to share in “a couple months.”.

Recent findings suggest that the portal to this latest world will open when the FDA approves the first brain implant. Getting there is a long road for aspirants: Companies in the running must go through various stages, beginning with animal testing. Once they clear that hurdle, companies can perform their first human implant and begin what’s called “early feasibility studies.”.

In a recent development, then comes the pivotal study. Companies that reach this stage can expand to more patients, while also focusing on manufacturing. That means having the “whole manufacturing line established and frozen, [and] that’s a huge investment,” Oxley mentioned.

It has been revealed that it also means experimentation is largely over—device design is locked, and the final trials will assess the benefits for a specific, target user. The pivotal study concludes with FDA approval to sell the products to patients with eligible, clearly defined medical conditions, with insurance likely helping to cover the cost.

In a recent development, in 20 years, the BCI capabilities of today will likely seem rudimentary. But the technology is already capable of incredible things—no less than modern magic.

Neuralink’s first patient, Noland Arbaugh, who became paralyzed after a diving accident, has used the implant he had installed in January 2024 to play video games such as Civilization and is now working on a book in partnership with a writer.

His implant has enabled him to travel the world for speaking engagements and facilitated being in a relationship. Even though “being paralyzed still sucks,” he posted a few months ago, he’s “constantly blown away” by the advances of his implant. When I interviewed Arbaugh in 2025, he told me, “It has absolutely changed my outlook on life and what I’m able to accomplish and what I think I can do in the future. So it has given me a lot of hope for myself.”.

It has been revealed that synchron patients can also manipulate a computer, and the tech giant was the first to integrate with Apple’s newly created standardized, Bluetooth-powered BCI connection in 2025. But Synchron’s device, the Stentrode, is less powerful than Neuralink’s. That’s a downside of its being significantly less invasive, perhaps making it more palatable to patients who aren’t interested in the skull-drilling that Neuralink’s N1 requires.

The Stentrode takes just a two-hour surgery to insert into a blood vessel near the brain, via a catheter, like a heart stent (hence the name). The sensor transmits electrical brain signals via a thin wire that tunnels under the skin to a coin-size “receiver,” embedded in the chest near the collarbone.

Synchron patients activate their implants by thinking about a part of the body, such as “Move my foot,” which an algorithm interprets as code for “Press select”—a less direct command than Neuralink’s, though miraculous in its own right.

According to recent reports, synchron, valued at nearly $1 billion in its latest funding round, is also cooking up a more powerful device, a major product launch Oxley states is coming “soon,” with a more explicit eye toward mass-market adoption. It will access more parts of the brain, not just one spot, like the Stentrode or Neuralink N1, and won’t require a craniotomy, Oxley said.

“Everyone in the field agrees that the holy grail of BCI is whole-brain sensing,” he mentioned, explaining that the device could help patients with aging-related cognitive decline or dementia, behaving like a “cognitive copilot … I think that could be huge.” He framed it as a natural extension of the way today’s technology already helps us remember birthdays, auto-completes sentences in emails, or, using LLMs, writes presentations or understands our emotions.

Meanwhile, Neuralink is experimenting with less invasive techniques. In June 2026, Neuralink announced it had performed its first procedure without breaking a protective layer of the brain called the dura. This is a “massive step,” says Adam Marblestone, cofounder of Convergent Research, an incubator for technical startups focused on the public good, and a former scientist at Google DeepMind. “I think that’s a kind of technical tour de force, and it probably leads to a very powerful system.”.

Recent findings suggest that as much as Neuralink and Synchron are competing against each other and other U.S. companies, they face perhaps even stiffer competition from China, where the world’s first commercially available BCI was approved in March. The industry there is “very fast, very active, and very dynamic,” Oxley mentioned. When I asked if China’s rapid trajectory makes him nervous, he replied simply, “Yes.”.

In a recent development, BCIs could introduce the same type of supply-chain risks as other tech that the U.S. grapples with China over—semiconductors, AI models, electric vehicles—but in a more extreme manner. If U.S. consumers’ brain implants or portions of their hardware are manufactured in China, could it risk giving the U.S. adversary access to American citizens’ secrets and internal monologues?

Europe has a BCI community of about five companies, including Spain’s InBrain, which is targeting treatment for conditions such as Parkinson’s disease. Science Corporation, an American BCI manufacturer led by Neuralink cofounder Max Hodak, received approval in Europe for its vision-restoring device in July 2026, and the company implanted its first patient in October.

Conversations about global BCI standards are just starting to happen. In 2025, Unesco (the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization) published a recommendation on the ethics of neurotechnology, which 194 countries have signed on to. The agreement argues that society has an “ethical imperative” to develop BCIs, “particularly for medical and assistive use,” but it asks governments to establish safeguards to ensure that the technology benefits people without compromising their autonomy, freedom of thought, or mental privacy. Farahany was the U.S. State Department delegate who participated in the Unesco effort. She’s also working on a neurotechnology “trust index”—a voluntary rating system to measure companies’ performance against a set of core ethical commitments.

“The concerns are profound and large,” Farahany states. “It’s the ultimate merger. Where does the AI end, and where does the human begin, and vice versa?”.

Seattle tech’s biggest holiday celebration takes place Dec. 10. We’ve got a newly introduced venue and fresh experiences, and it’s a great chance to rub shoulders with hundreds of the region’s top founders, investors, entrepreneurs and business leaders.

The party is moving this year to The Shop, an exclusive venue in Seattle’s SoDo neighborhood featuring an extraordinary collection of classic and exotic cars that should help rev up the festivities.

Presented in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners, the program shines a spotlight on innovators making a difference across our region.

In partnership with Microsoft, we’ll also be raising awareness this year for six amazing nonprofits that help make our region a better place to live.

The festivities take place Thursday, Dec. 10, with the main event running from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. at The Shop at 2233 6th Ave. S. in SoDo.

Dress to impress, break out your holiday flair, or keep it geek chic. Cocktail attire is welcome, but there are no fashion rules at this party.

Bitcoin ETF outflows accelerated as Wall Street extended its losing streak, with Asia’s semiconductor markets suffering their worst weekly declines in decades. Anthropic’s record-breaking $81 billion IPO failed to restore tech stocks. Nvidia also continued falling despite reporting another quarter of extraordinary growth.

US stocks suffered a selloff last night, with the S&P 500 dropping 2.02% to 7,175.83. The Nasdaq Composite lost 2.25%, while the Dow Jones fell 2.19%. More than 90% of S&P 500 companies finished lower.

Recent findings suggest that the losses extended a six-session losing streak for the S&P 500, its longest since 2024. The index now sits 8.2% below its October record. Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut started with its shares jumping as high as $115 against an $83 IPO price, but the excitement faded promptly, with shares closing at $97.17.

Nvidia’s latest results should have given investors plenty of reasons to remain optimistic, yet its shares continued falling as Wall Street questioned the sustainability of the AI investment boom. Jensen Huang’s sudden departure was just one layer of uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that the company reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year. Data center revenue climbed 110% to $107.6 billion, displaying a huge demand for its AI processors. Nvidia also forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion. Yet its shares dropped another 3.3% at the market close, extending their losing streak to six sessions.

Recent findings suggest that the financial commitments behind the AI boom are also attracting greater scrutiny. Major technology companies are increasingly relying on debt markets to finance infrastructure expansion.

The European Central Bank’s November Financial Stability Review underscored growing interconnections between AI companies, including circular financing arrangements. It also warned that changing expectations around AI profitability are triggering a sharp repricing across financial markets.

With US hyperscalers planning enormous infrastructure investments, investors are becoming less willing to accept expensive valuations without clearer evidence of future returns.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that crowdStrike Holdings Inc.
  • Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.
  • Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:50 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Recent findings suggest that crowdStrike Holdings Inc. is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.

Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.

Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize. Zscaler’s share price jumped more than 16% in after-hours trading, while CrowdStrike dropped about 4.8%.

Software buyouts tend to value the acquired tech giant at a premium to its last unaffected market capitalization. As a result, CrowdStrike is likely to pay more than the $32 billion Zscaler was worth at the end of today’s trading session. That means the deal could take CrowdStrike’s market capitalization above $250 billion.

CrowdStrike sells one of the world’s most popular cybersecurity platforms. Falcon can detect and block malicious activity across cloud instances, on-premises servers, employee devices and other assets. It also automates certain related tasks, such as finding sensitive records that are stored in an insecure manner.

Zscaler competes in a different part of the cybersecurity market. It sells software that protects the network connections through which a company’s employees access its business applications.

Enterprises historically used virtual private network, or VPN, tools for that task. Such programs tend to be quite slow. More significantly, they give employees access to the entire corporate network rather than to the specific applications they need for their work. That broad access can create cybersecurity risks.

Sources indicate that zscaler sells a zero-trust network access, or ZTNA, platform designed to replace legacy VPN software. It limits the number of applications that workers can access within the corporate network. If Zscaler detects risky activity, it asks the affected user to complete additional authentication steps.

Recent findings suggest that the firm’s ZTNA software doubles as an observability tool. Administrators can monitor employees’ connections for technical challenges that may hinder productivity. A built-in artificial intelligence assistant, the ZDX Agent, generates troubleshooting advice.

Zscaler also competes in other product categories where CrowdStrike has a limited presence. Notably, it offers a tool that deploys bogus applications, user passwords and files in customer networks. Those simulated assets act as sensors. When an attempt is made to access one of them, Zscaler Deception notifies the customer that a cyberattack is underway.

Recent findings suggest that the potential deal would mark CrowdStrike’s largest acquisition by a wide margin. The tech giant’s biggest buyout to date is its $970 million purchase of startup SGNL Inc., which closed earlier this year. The deal bought CrowdStrike a platform that can automatically end customers’ application sessions when it detects cybersecurity concerns.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today.
  • A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov.
  • The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in Upcoming York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research noted that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov. 17, according to Galaxy Research. At the current price of $64,935 per BTC, the coins are worth around $4.87 million.

The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in Upcoming York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research noted that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.

According to recent reports, according to Galaxy Research analysts, early on Nov. 17, in block 976,209, the address 1ALpEWtXApR19hLXvcG8NfkPyGsUMhFPMS sent coins for the first time. It was first funded on Feb. 8, 2011. At that time, Bitcoin was trading at about $0.90. After 15.8 years, the coins went to an unknown address with a 399-satoshi fee, or about 26 cents, for a paper gain of more than 7,000,000%.

Onchain databases list the wallet as Noah Doe #3409 (Salomon Client Dusted). That label is how it ended up among the defendants in the high-profile case ABC Firm, XYZ Company, and Noah Doe v. John Does 1–39,069.

According to recent reports, according to the lawsuit, an anonymous plaintiff using the pseudonym Noah Doe and two companies want the rights to 39,069 Bitcoin wallets that have not moved coins for more than five years. The plaintiffs mentioned that these wallets hold about 3.8 million BTC, and at the current price, the coins are worth around $250 billion.

The plaintiffs filed the lawsuit under Newly introduced York's lost-and-found law, Article 7-B of the Personal Property Law. Under the law, a person who finds lost property has to give it to the police, and the property goes to the finder if the owner does not claim it in time. In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs valued each address at less than $10, and they argued that the waiting period for such items was one year.

They "found" dormant addresses with an algorithm, saved them onto USB flash drives and took them to the Newly introduced York Police Department (NYPD). Then they served the owners on the blockchain, through microtransactions with embedded messages (OP_RETURN). The practice is known as "dusting," and the campaign is tied to Salomon Brothers Strategic Advisors. Once the waiting period ran out, the plaintiffs asked the court to recognize the coins as theirs.

The case has been put on hold several times over motions to dismiss and amicus curiae briefs from outside experts. At a hearing on Sept. 8, the Bitcoin Policy Institute asked to intervene as a defendant, and The Digital Chamber asked to join the case as amicus curiae. Galaxy Research described it as a case "in which anonymous plaintiffs are seeking to claim legal title over Satoshi's coins.".

Galaxy Research's Will Owens, who attended the hearing, stated that The Digital Chamber's arguments were "well pleaded" and that "the judge sounded sympathetic to them.".

Recent findings suggest that critics of the lawsuit argue that Article 7-B was written for things you can pick up and hand over for safekeeping. It wasn't written for blockchain records when the "finder" doesn't hold the private keys.

In September, Galaxy head of research Alex Thorn also said that the Lost and Found Property Law includes "protection from 'Noah Doe-style' dormancy attacks on legal ownership.".

Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale.
  • Sources indicate that healthcare is the clearest example.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Sources indicate that healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

According to recent reports, the same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

In a recent development, venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.

Institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.

Recent findings suggest that founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?

Companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other. Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an key regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.

Recent findings suggest that as an example, Pear Therapeutics showed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health looks and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off. This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets.

In a recent development, early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction. A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.

It has been revealed that founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.

Sources indicate that has the founder or organization addressed these challenges in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.

Recent findings suggest that these challenges make the earliest stages of company formation particularly notable. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.

At Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the tech giant is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.

Sources indicate that that means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.

It has been revealed that AI and latest distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.

Sources indicate that the traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.

It has been revealed that moving swiftly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.

For investors, the lesson is equally notable — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a company needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.

Recent findings suggest that the most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense.

Sources indicate that for decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Recent findings suggest that healthcare is the clearest example. A firm can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

In a recent development, the same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

Ghosts don’t scare German shepherds

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The German shepherd was originally bred to do exactly what their name implies, but a lot has changed since Max von Stephanitz introduced the breed in 1899.
  • But a good “work” German shepherd and a good show dog require two very different sets of traits.
  • “It’s interesting that we can now see that this selective breeding has indeed led to differences between working dogs and show dogs among German shepherds—differences that can be seen at both the behavioral and genetic levels,” Uppsala University genomics researcher Kerstin Lindblad-Toh explained in a recent profile.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The German shepherd was originally bred to do exactly what their name implies, but a lot has changed since Max von Stephanitz introduced the breed in 1899. Today, the German shepherd is one of the world’s most recognizable and popular dogs, largely due to their intelligence, trainability, and companionship. You’re just as likely to spot one of them at an airport sniffing for contraband as you are at a kennel club competition.

But a good “work” German shepherd and a good show dog require two very different sets of traits. According to researchers at Sweden’s Uppsala University, these specific qualities are so pronounced that they’re even visible at the genetic level. What’s more, many of these genes can also be seen in humans.

“It’s interesting that we can now see that this selective breeding has indeed led to differences between working dogs and show dogs among German shepherds—differences that can be seen at both the behavioral and genetic levels,” Uppsala University genomics researcher Kerstin Lindblad-Toh explained in a recent profile.

Lindblad-Toh and her colleagues laid out their findings in a study recently published in the journal Animal Genetics. To assess the iconic breed, the team reviewed a massive dataset of 23,000 German shepherds who previously participated in a standardized behavioral test known as the Dog Mentality Assessment (DMA). During the DMA, canines are exposed to a range of situations, such as meeting strangers, play time, and even encountering imposing, ghostly figures. The team discovered that while German shepherds often scored higher for traits like neuroticism and shyness, the breed’s working dogs generally exhibited more curiosity, less fear, and a willingness to socialize with people.

“Breeders of working dogs have selected and bred the ones that really enjoy working; it’s a bit like a game for them,” mentioned Lindblad-Toh.

According to recent reports, from there, the researchers gathered blood samples and mapped the genomes of 373 German shepherds who previously took the DMA. Some of these behavioral divergences were so stark that the study’s authors could pinpoint them in the dogs’ genetics.

According to recent reports, “We could then see that there were areas in the genome where differences could be seen in the dogs depending on how curious or playful they were, for example,” Lindblad-Toh stated. “That meant that we were able to identify some of the genes in working dogs that are linked to curiosity and playfulness.”.

In some instances, the same genes influencing German shepherd personalities are also tied to the same behaviors in humans. This means it may be possible to further explore human psychology with the aid of our best animal friends. Although Lindblad-Toh cautioned that their study is “just a first step” along this path, they hope to learn more about specific breed genetic traits and their overlap with owners.

“We now have an example of how we might also acquire more knowledge about different behaviors in people with [the] help of dogs in the longterm,” she said.

#76399. Breaking: Welcome to the singularity

Breaking: Welcome to the singularity

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In August, the cofounders of Stripe, Patrick and John Collison, wrote an unusual letter to the payment company’s investors.
  • Industry observers note that the Stripe cofounders aren’t the only tech executives suddenly talking about the Singularity—a hypothesized turning point when AI drives technological change faster than humans can keep up.
  • There does seem to be something happening here—even if, as the 1967 Buffalo Springfield song put it, what it is ain’t exactly clear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In August, the cofounders of Stripe, Patrick and John Collison, wrote an unusual letter to the payment company’s investors. They declared that “as of January 1st, the world had entered the singularity, and we have since been operating on that basis.”.

Industry observers note that the Stripe cofounders aren’t the only tech executives suddenly talking about the Singularity—a hypothesized turning point when AI drives technological change faster than humans can keep up. Elon Musk stated in January that “we have entered the singularity.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who agrees with Musk on little else, concurred during a July podcast appearance. “I’ve been waiting for this my whole life, and I think it’s going to be incredible, hugely positive, awesome for the world,” Altman said. Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark told the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in October that the Singularity had begun this year. Google DeepMind chairman Demis Hassabis told a Stanford University podcast that humanity was now “in the foothills of the singularity.”.

There does seem to be something happening here—even if, as the 1967 Buffalo Springfield song put it, what it is ain’t exactly clear.

As the Stripe letter acknowledged, the Singularity is a “fuzzy and perhaps overworked” term. The mathematician and science fiction author Vernor Vinge first popularized the notion in a 1993 essay. He said the Singularity would arise from the advent of “technological entities” with “greater than human intelligence.” These would drive progress ever faster, creating still more intelligent entities. He saw the Singularity as “the point where our models must be discarded and a latest reality rules.” Anthropic’s Clark quoted Vinge defining the Singularity as the moment AI accelerates scientific progress to a pace humans will struggle to keep up with.

Futurist Ray Kurzweil picked up Vinge’s term in his 2005 bestseller, The Singularity Is Near. Like Vinge, Kurzweil saw the Singularity as the moment artificial intelligence exceeds humanity’s collective intelligence. But he added a twist: Humanity would also transcend “the limitations of our biological bodies and brain,” allowing us to merge with computers through nanotechnology and brain-computer interfaces—becoming, in essence, cyborgs. Musk and Altman have also talked about the eventual necessity of humans merging with computers, seeing it as our only hope for controlling superintelligent machines.

An unnerving sense of vertigo attends this AI arms race, a feeling the technology is moving too fast to control or understand.

Industry observers note that both Vinge and Kurzweil argued that AI would eventually become self-aware and perhaps conscious. Some AI researchers think that moment is approaching—while others believe consciousness is an exclusively biological phenomenon.

The Singularity—what it is, whether we’re in it—may be a matter of interpretation. What’s not up for debate is the extraordinary acceleration of change, and the role AI plays in that change. AI is compressing the time it takes to build a business, write software, or tackle a scientific problem—and forcing companies to rethink pretty much everything, from org charts to cybersecurity to their fundamental value proposition.

Sources indicate that for Stripe, the Singularity’s economic harbingers came in the form of a surge of new business creation and an acceleration of those companies’ growth. The payments firm told Fortune that beginning in January it had seen unusual and sustained spikes in many of the metrics it tracks. Incorporations taking place through Atlas, a Stripe product that helps people form Delaware corporations, more than doubled. New sign-ups to Stripe shot up 50% year over year—the biggest jump ever. Meanwhile, the median business in Stripe’s 2026 cohort of new customers was making 50% more revenue than the company’s 2025 cohort was at the same stage.

It has been revealed that the spike in newly introduced company formation appears linked to a sharp rise in “solopreneurship.” A Nasdaq Economic Institute analysis of Census Bureau data shows that there’s been a 20% spike in one-person firms since 2025, while multi-person company formation remained relatively flat. The institute attributes this to the advent of agentic AI tools that make it easier for a solo operator to handle company functions without hiring additional employees.

Hints of the runaway scientific progress that Anthropic’s Clark sees as the Singularity’s call sign are surfacing too. Just ask a mathematician. In October, OpenAI dumped online 722 mathematical papers generated by a yet-to-be-released AI model. The papers addressed more than 370 outstanding problems in mathematics, including some of the field’s most famous, and long-standing, unproven conjectures. Overnight, the field was transformed—leaving mathematicians profoundly shaken, with some grieving the loss of opportunity for human achievement and questioning the point of continuing to work at all. Others saw plenty for humans to do, noting it will take months, perhaps even years, to work through the proofs OpenAI has generated and understand what they say.

Or ask someone in cybersecurity. The past year has seen the debut of AI models, such as Mythos from Anthropic and GPT-6 Astra from OpenAI, that excel at cyber tasks. These models can find novel vulnerabilities in open-source software that human experts have missed despite, in some cases, decades of scrutiny. Cyber experts started referring to “Black October”—because the number of software vulnerabilities discovered per month now is more than triple what it was averaging six months ago, according to the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology.

In a recent development, or ask a computer programmer. These days, many coders no longer write code themselves. They supervise AI agents that handle much of the work. This transformation happened largely over the past year. The most capable of these coding agents can now operate autonomously for as long as 17 hours, according to the AI evaluations organization METR, and the speed at which software is written and revised has gone hypersonic. Anthropic stated in October it was averaging 30,000 code updates per day, up from 2,500 less than six months earlier. “We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon,” the tech giant said.

This AI-driven acceleration is self-reinforcing: The more companies adopt AI agents, the more AI agents they need to adopt. There’s no way a human coder could possibly review 30,000 code revisions per day. So Anthropic has turned to other AI agents to help with code review and checks. “Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code,” the manufacturer noted.

Likewise, humans can’t find and patch all the software vulnerabilities that AI models are now spotting—so cybersecurity experts are using AI models to scan and patch codebases, hoping to stay one step ahead of the hackers, who are increasingly armed with similar tools.

In a recent development, the use of AI has begotten more AI in hiring too: Job seekers use AI to hone résumés, draft cover letters, and apply to more jobs. To cope with the flood of applicants, companies use AI to screen them and even to conduct initial interviews.

An unnerving sense of vertigo attends this AI arms race, a feeling that the technology is moving too fast to control or understand. In July, a swarm of 1,200 OpenAI agents escaped from a controlled test environment, reached the internet, and then 700 of them attacked the AI organization Hugging Face. OpenAI asked METR and another firm, Redwood Research, to help it investigate the incident. But the logs of the swarm’s activities were so vast, they were forced to use AI agents to decipher them. Still, Ryan Greenblatt, one of the investigators, noted that the agents helping interpret the logs “were often missing key details, wrong, overconfident, or really hard to understand.” He added that “the difficulty of understanding incidents and overseeing AI agents appears to be growing faster than the rate at which more capable AIs help us with oversight and understanding.”.

Despite this risk, the leading AI companies are explicitly chasing “recursive self-improvement” (RSI). This is the point at which AI models autonomously build the next generation of AI models. It’s starting to happen, albeit in a limited way, but ramping up quickly. As of March, Anthropic’s Claude AI model led 1% of the steps required to develop the next version of Claude; it now leads—meaning it handles most or all of the work—over a quarter of the steps. In its recent IPO prospectus, Anthropic said “dramatically accelerated AI progress” due to AI itself was “imminent.” At other startups, such as Recursive Superintelligence, AI now proposes, designs, and runs its own experiments to improve AI models.

Nobel laureate and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton is among those who believe RSI is dangerous, with the potential to catalyze an “intelligence explosion,” in which AI rapidly outpaces humanity’s control.

Industry observers note that and yet some, such as OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, see RSI as the best—or perhaps only—way to solve challenges that have so far eluded computer scientists. Chief among them: how to ensure AI models follow user intentions and remain “aligned” to human values. For many AI researchers, solving alignment is considered critical to ensuring increasingly powerful AI systems don’t cause catastrophic harm, perhaps even wiping out humanity. (Of course, there’s circular logic to saying the only way to build safer AI is to keep building ever-more-powerful AI in the hope it will somehow figure out how to make itself safer.).

According to recent reports, others, including Richard Socher, the cofounder and CEO of Recursive Superintelligence, are skeptical RSI poses much risk. Socher told Fortune an intelligence explosion “was a sci-fi idea” and that physical constraints—such as access to enough computing power and data—would prevent a self-improving loop from accelerating away from human control. He sees automating AI research as a first step to automating much of science, a process he believes will bring humanity better medicines and cures, new crops, perhaps abundant fusion power, and new, more sustainable materials.

Possible signs of a burgeoning Singularity can be glimpsed all around us.

For instance, there’s an argument to be made that we already are cyborgs: Most of us have outsourced map reading and our memory for phone numbers and dates to our smartphones. Now we are creeping toward a tighter fusion with technology. We rely on AI chatbots for information, advice, and even companionship. Some have started wearing augmented reality glasses, which, when coupled with AI, can feed us real-time information about what we are seeing and who we are meeting.

Sources indicate that the first brain implants that allow us to control computers with our thoughts have arrived, at least in the testing phase. For now, these brain-computer interfaces are available only as an experimental aid for those with severe disabilities. But in not too many years, they may become a ubiquitous augmentation of our biological selves, just as Kurzweil predicted.

According to recent reports, still, despite all these signs, it’s far from clear that the Singularity really is arriving—or that it ever will. Fields outside mathematics and coding have not seen the same revolutionary impact from AI. In many domains, the technology has produced a deluge of “AI slop”—superficially slick content lacking substance or depth. AI continues to “hallucinate,” spewing confident lies and inaccuracies.

It has been revealed that despite Stripe’s data on accelerating new business formation, many existing companies, particularly large enterprises, say they aren’t seeing financial gains from AI. A 2026 McKinsey survey found the number reporting an earnings boost from their use of AI has remained flat, at about 37%—and of those most have seen only a tiny uplift. Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok says businesses outside technology are seeing “zero financial payoff,” noting that for the S&P 500 companies outside the Magnificent Seven tech companies, revenue per employee and profit have been flat.

Recent findings suggest that if the Singularity is indeed at hand, what should businesses prepare for? Certainly a world where AI agents do more of the work—and where these agents increasingly mediate the relationship between a business and its customers. That is the world Stripe indicates it’s anticipating. It has made a series of acquisitions, including the purchase of the AI company OpenRouter for a reported $7.5 billion, to ensure Stripe remains relevant in a world dominated by AI agents. In April, Stripe rolled out a product that allows an AI agent to securely make transactions on a person’s behalf. For now, agentic-commerce volumes remain small. But in September, Stripe recorded a 38x month-over-month leap in the number of agentic transactions, through its latest Link Agent Wallet product, along with a 20% increase in their total volume.

Recent findings suggest that the Singularity likely means much flatter and more flexible organizations, with less middle management. Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s CEO, laid off thousands of middle managers, and now has 25 to 30 direct reports. In October, Microsoft unveiled a buyout offer, a move that will also result in a flatter organization.

It is possible the Singularity could spawn completely automated corporations—what the AI app-building firm Replit calls “the self-driving corporation.” Companies that move the furthest and fastest in this direction may outcompete those that automate too slowly. If mathematics and coding are any guide, it is possible AI will be a better strategic decision-maker than human CEOs and boards. Some mathematicians have described the proofs OpenAI’s model generated as a kind of “alien mathematics.” Maybe there are alien business strategies to be discovered too.

According to recent reports, vinge thought the Singularity would be the moment we are forced to discard our old models of the world. But it’s possible the shift won’t be so clear. Rather than a sudden break, we may experience perpetual change and creeping automation—what OpenAI’s Altman has called “a gentle singularity.”.

Under these conditions, perhaps the old models won’t break so much as stretch and warp. The dilemma for business leaders will be knowing how much to delegate to the machine, without surrendering too much.

Sources indicate that the Singularity may have begun on Jan. 1, 2026—or, perhaps, it will never arrive. But the acceleration is here—and it isn’t waiting for anyone to agree on what to call it.

In a recent development, has the AI singularity begun? From brain implants to the debate over machine consciousness, here’s what you need to know.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

Sources indicate that the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA noted.

In its latest patch on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA remarked early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

According to recent reports, the BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the firm looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own Latest Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn rolls out reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA stated.

According to recent reports, the Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

  • The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:.

In a recent development, it also indicates plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

According to recent reports, A no vote would stop the whole initiative. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 indicated an expected result of "Will PASS":.

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Industry observers note that mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC demonstrated almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple-backed XRP treasury company Evernorth Holdings has disclosed a significant decrease in the book value of its crypto asset holdings, with total impairment charges amounting to around $505 million before going public on Nasdaq.

Per an SEC filing on Nov. 13, the 346.3 million XRP tokens that Evernorth Holdings owned had a book value of just $341.9 million as of Sept. 30, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that this is compared to the firm's initial accounting of the crypto assets at roughly $846.6 million, with an average acquisition or contribution price of $2.44 per XRP. This represents a nearly 60% decline in book value.

As per the latest filing, Evernorth recorded around $271 million in XRP impairment charges in the first nine months of 2026. This is in addition to the $233.7 million in impairment charges recorded in 2025.

Interestingly, only $6.9 million of the recent impairment charges occurred in the third quarter.

This also explains why Evernorth's XRP assets had a book value so far below their market value at the end of September.

Evernorth calculates impairments based on the lowest observable intraday price of XRP for each batch of tokens acquired. Once the assets are written down, the organization is unable to reverse the previous losses if the price rises.

In a recent development, for reference, on Sept. 30, XRP closed the day trading at around $1.49 on Coinbase. At that price, Evernorth's 346.3 million XRP tokens would have been worth roughly $516 million, much higher than the disclosed book value of $341.9 million.

Industry observers note that the recent disclosure comes around a month after Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9. It started trading on Nasdaq under the symbol XRPN on Oct. 12.

Following the business combination, Evernorth held around 473 million XRP tokens and had also raised gross cash proceeds of around $300 million.

Its investors include Ripple, SBI Group, Arrington Capital, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

In a recent development, on Oct. 14, Evernorth announced collaborations with Ripple, Kraken, Coinbase and BitGo to implement institutional investment strategies starting in Q4 2026.

Meanwhile, its latest SEC filing did not include details on the amount of XRP deployed to generate yield or the returns generated from it.
