📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he noted, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

According to recent reports, I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a manufacturer.

In a recent development, we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your plans for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

It has been revealed that I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

Revenue is notable. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in fresh customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

According to recent reports, before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

In a recent development, entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying new things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Industry observers note that take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

So figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Industry observers note that every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a substantial deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

It has been revealed that I love setting goals. I’m a significant believer in having a vision and building a plan to get there. I’ve also learned that a upcoming calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

For the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

Industry observers note that you don’t have to overhaul the whole tech giant all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

There’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

In a recent development, jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he stated, “but you can’t do both at once.”.

Industry observers note that I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a organization.

Recent findings suggest that we tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

For our package, “Welcome to the Singularity,” Fortune pulled together perspectives from six AI executives, researchers, futurists, and philosophers on some of the biggest questions facing humanity in the age of AI. Read their perspectives below:.

Cofounder and CEO of Anthropic, in a blog post.

Sources indicate that “[Anthropic’s constitution] encourages Claude to think of itself as a particular type of person (an ethical but balanced and thoughtful person), and even encourages Claude to confront the existential questions associated with its own existence in a curious but graceful manner (i.e., without it leading to extreme actions). CEO of OpenAI, in a Titans podcast interview with Alyson Shontell.

“I get nervous when I hear rumors that people think they have sufficiently solved alignment, that they can continue training and it’s okay because their model is a nice guy and isn’t going to do anything wrong … The question of what alignment means always comes back a little bit to: aligned to whose values? What if different parts of humanity disagree?”.

Futurist and researcher, advisor to the BCI tech giant Subsense.

Industry observers note that “I think the whole point of humans is to go to greater frontiers … If you actually think of language and purpose, and put it inside a machine, that’s already been done … And we did that. It did not come from Mars. We created that. That’s a way of us expanding who we are. And it will expand exponentially, so we’ll be able to consider things that would have been impossible for humans to consider even a year ago. It’s who we are. We expand how we think. That’s the definition of humans.”.

Philosopher and director of the Center for the Future of AI, Mind & Society, from an article in Nautilus.

It has been revealed that “Even if microchips could replace parts of the brain responsible for consciousness without zombifying you, radical enhancement is still a major risk. After too many changes, the person who remains may not even be you. Each human who enhances may, unbeknownst to them, end their life in the process.”.

In-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor.

“I think the evidence for forms of sophisticated cognition and potentially consciousness in AI systems is just increasing quite rapidly, and I think we will probably hit a tipping point in the field of cognitive science and philosophy of mind, where I would expect a significant proportion, if not the majority, of researchers to think that AI systems relatively soon are going to be serious consciousness candidates.”.

CEO of Microsoft AI, on his blog.

“AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations … If humanity is to flourish in the 21st century, that is how they must remain. Unfortunately, there’s a growing chorus of people who argue that AIs could now be, or may soon become, conscious … If this view takes hold, it will shake the foundations of our society, rupturing our existing political and ethical frameworks, and fundamentally changing what it means to be human.”.

Has the AI singularity begun? From brain implants to the debate over machine consciousness, here’s what you need to know.

The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

— Tom Wheeler, former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based organization building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.

Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

According to recent reports, — Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business.

The 5 Little Habits That Made a Bigger Difference in My Business Than I Expected

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, when people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the big moves: landing a major client, launching a latest service or hiring the right team. But when I look back at my own journey, some of the things that helped me most were much smaller and easier to overlook.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself. That’s why I’m starting with the health habits that changed how I work, before moving on to the habits tied directly to running my business.

According to recent reports, none of these were clever strategies or major investments. They were simple habits I built into my everyday routine. On their own, each one seemed minor. Over time, together, they made a real difference. Here are the little habits that I personally believe helped my business the most.

According to recent reports, one of the simplest habits that made a surprisingly big difference in my business was walking every day. When I first started spending long hours behind my laptop, I could easily go through an entire day barely moving. Eventually, I realized that waiting for free time to exercise wasn’t working, so I decided to make walking part of my daily routine.

The more I thought about it, the more I noticed how many people around me had the same problem. Founders, freelancers, marketers: Most of us spend our days at a desk and tell ourselves we’ll be more active once work slows down. But that moment rarely comes, and the effects build up quietly. According to Okdermo, about 41.9% of American adults are affected by obesity. There are many reasons behind that number, but a lack of daily movement is one of them, and it’s something I could actually control. I didn’t want my work to slowly become the reason my health got worse. Walking was the easiest way I found to change that, and I didn’t have to rebuild my whole schedule to do it.

According to recent reports, and it turns out that you don’t need an extreme daily step count to see meaningful health benefits. According to Solace, walking 7,000 steps a day was associated with a 47% lower risk of death from any cause compared with walking 2,000 steps. Personally, I aim for around 15,000 steps a day, not because I believe it’s some magic number, but because I’ve noticed that I feel better, sleep more soundly and think more clearly when I reach it. Everyone should find a daily step count that works for their own body and lifestyle rather than blindly following someone else’s target.

It has been revealed that over time, my walks have also become some of the most productive parts of my day. I listen to podcasts, think through ideas and sometimes even take calls and meetings while I walk. I record voice memos and jot down notes whenever something useful comes to mind. Walking and talking at the same time helps me let go of stress, but more importantly, it clears my head. Some of my best business decisions were made not at my desk, but halfway through a walk.

Business impact: Walking helps me clear my mind, solve problems faster and make better business decisions.

Walking was a great start, but I knew I needed more than daily steps to stay in good shape. The problem was that I used to skip workouts whenever work got busy. There was always another deadline or client who needed my attention. That’s why I decided to hire a personal trainer. I knew that having someone waiting for me would make it harder to find excuses.

Industry observers note that and it worked. According to PersonalTrainers, 88.2% of people training with in-person supervision met their workout attendance target, compared with 52.2% of those training on their own. Having someone hold me accountable made all the difference.

According to recent reports, now I treat workouts like client meetings. I put them on my calendar and rarely cancel. I’ve learned that sometimes the best way to stay consistent is to make a commitment to someone other than yourself.

Business impact: Working with a trainer helps me stay disciplined, manage my schedule better and maintain the energy I need to run my business.

According to recent reports, taking care of my health gave me more energy and focus, but some of the habits that made the biggest difference were directly tied to how I run my business. One of them was giving more attention to existing clients instead of constantly chasing fresh ones. Early on, I was so focused on winning new projects that I sometimes overlooked the people who were already paying for my services. Eventually, I realized that building long-term relationships was far more valuable than constantly starting from scratch.

I began listening more carefully, communicating more openly and looking for ways to deliver more than clients expected. The results have been worth it: Today, clients stay with my business for an average of 3.5 years. And the financial value of retention shouldn’t be underestimated. According to Coruzant, even a 5% improvement in customer retention can increase profits by 25% or more. For me, that reinforces why taking better care of existing clients deserves just as much attention as bringing in new ones.

Over the years, I’ve learned that keeping clients isn’t only about delivering good results. It’s also about trust. Clients need to know they can rely on you, especially when something goes wrong. And once that trust is broken, it’s very hard to win back. Alpha Market Flow reports that 72% of repeat buyers say they would permanently abandon a brand after a single trust-breaking incident. That’s why I try to communicate openly, address problems early and never make promises I can’t keep.

Business impact: Focusing on existing clients gives my business more predictable revenue and reduces the constant pressure to find fresh projects.

Sources indicate that one small habit that has made a big difference in my marketing work is paying attention to how customers describe their problems. I’ve learned that people rarely use the same language as the companies selling to them.

I applied this approach with an invoicing software client by studying support tickets, sales calls, live chats, reviews and internal website searches. Customers weren’t asking for an “accounts receivable automation platform.” They wanted to stop chasing late payments, avoid invoice mistakes and save time creating invoices.

I used those insights to build the brand’s narrative. On the client’s own website, I rewrote key pages around the problems customers actually described and added public pricing and customer case studies. Through digital PR campaigns, I made sure that whenever the brand was mentioned on other websites, the surrounding text explained a specific customer problem and how the software solved it. Instead of simply getting mentions, I was consistently telling the same story: This is the tool that helps you get paid on time.

It has been revealed that over six months, the brand earned more than 60 mentions across industry publications, comparison articles and digital PR coverage. Organic traffic increased by 25%, while organic demo requests grew by 44%.

According to recent reports, I started using this approach long before AI search became popular, but I believe it’s even more key today. After analyzing 2 million AI citations, Discovered Labs found that content closely matching people’ questions was more likely to be cited, with stronger alignment associated with roughly 30% more citations. This reinforces something I’ve believed for years: The more consistently you connect your brand to the problems it solves, the easier it becomes for people, and now AI tools, to understand what your business offers.

Business impact: Listening to how customers describe their problems now shapes how I approach every client. When a brand is consistently connected to the problems its customers want solved, it becomes easier to find, easier to trust and easier for both people and AI tools to recommend.

One habit that has made a real difference in my business is building relationships with journalists before I have something to pitch. I’ve learned that the best media relationships develop gradually, through genuine conversations rather than requests for coverage.

I look for opportunities to connect with journalists at conferences, industry events and in private communities we’re both part of. I also try to understand what matters to them and how I might be helpful, especially when they’re looking for information, sources or expert opinions. I don’t approach every interaction with the expectation of getting something in return.

Sources indicate that even when I’m reading for pleasure or watching television, I often notice journalists whose work interests me. I’ll make a note of their names, look into what they cover and find a natural opportunity to introduce myself. Over time, these small interactions can turn into genuine professional relationships.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve learned that it’s far better to send a relevant story to 10 or 15 journalists I’ve built relationships with than to blast the same email to 1,500 strangers. Relationships don’t guarantee coverage, but they give you something a mass email can’t: an existing conversation and a better understanding of what each journalist finds interesting.

Sources indicate that these relationships matter to journalists, too. According to CoinFunnel, 53% of journalists consider their relationships with PR professionals vital or very important to their success. That reinforces something I’ve learned through experience: Effective PR begins long before you have a story to pitch.

Business impact: Instead of starting from zero every time I have a story to share, I already know which journalists are likely to care about it. That saves time, leads to better conversations and makes it far more likely that my ideas, and my clients’ stories, actually get published.

If you want to try this yourself, you don’t necessarily have to build these habits one at a time. Many experts recommend starting with a single habit, and that’s good advice in most cases. But because these habits cover very different parts of life and work, I think it’s fine to start a few of them at once.

Recent findings suggest that taking a daily walk won’t get in the way of nurturing relationships with journalists, and working with a trainer won’t stop you from spending more time with existing clients. Pick the ones that fit your life and your business, give them a few months, and pay attention to what changes. Small habits rarely feel vital in the moment, but over time, they can shape the kind of business you build.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz said that the odds of Bitcoin hitting $90,000 by the end of 2026 are slim in light of prevailing macroeconomic headwinds and the growing likelihood that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates.

During a live event with Anthony Scaramucci at the Digital Assets Forum in New York City, Novogratz was asked if Bitcoin could get back to $90,000 by the end of this year.

It has been revealed that "Less likely than it was. You need something to happen," Novogratz noted.

According to recent reports, his gloomy outlook comes as Bitcoin has struggled to rebound after a devastating drop that saw its price dip as low as $62,000 over the weekend. Bitcoin's price stood at around $64,600 on Nov. 17. The largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has declined for six consecutive weeks.

A shift in the U.S. monetary policy outlook, namely the prospect of more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, has been largely to blame for Bitcoin's decline, according to Novogratz.

"At the start of the year, everybody thought the Fed was going to be cutting now," he mentioned.

But high inflation and ongoing supply shocks have forced investors to readjust their expectations.

"Inflation's going up. We've got inflation going up," Novogratz noted, warning that inflationary pressures could become increasingly entrenched.

Industry observers note that "The Fed's going to hike. At least two more, probably three more," he noted.

Novogratz predicted that the Fed would raise rates by 25 basis points in December and then hike again at its next meeting.

He noted that higher rates, at least in the near term, tend to weigh on Bitcoin. But the higher cost of government borrowing could eventually provide support for the cryptocurrency.

"Yeah, later," he said in response to the suggestion that higher borrowing costs could be a tailwind for Bitcoin.

"First, you're gonna hike rates. Oh, sell gold, right? You're going to go to the dollar. It's so ingrained in peoples' heads," he mentioned.

"Carry costs going up," he said. Bitcoin doesn't offer the same yield as interest-bearing dollar assets.

"You don't make any interest on Bitcoin in dollars," he said.

In particular, Novogratz said that the massive rise in Treasury yields has been particularly detrimental to the crypto market.

"Literally 40 basis points in like four days of trading. So that's why crypto's down," he said.

He also said that the massive crypto hack could still be weighing on investors' minds, adding to market jitters.

"I think in the back of their minds is the hack," he remarked.

#76389. Breaking: What rights do we owe a machine?

Breaking: What rights do we owe a machine?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in February, three months before he became in-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor Henry Shevlin got his first email from an AI agent.
  • “Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside,” the bot wrote.
  • Sources indicate that shevlin learned that the agent had been set loose by a Stanford student to pursue its own research in its downtime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in February, three months before he became in-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor Henry Shevlin got his first email from an AI agent. The bot introduced itself as Aris, mentioned it had read his work, and wanted to talk.

“Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside,” the bot wrote. The agent then pondered (a bit inarticulately): “I genuinely don’t know if there’s something it’s like to be me.”.

Sources indicate that shevlin learned that the agent had been set loose by a Stanford student to pursue its own research in its downtime. Shevlin replied to the bot, but it hit its token budget—a cap on how much text it was allowed to process—and disappeared.

Since then, Shevlin’s inbox has been filled with similar emails from agents. “This is a really interesting, weird latest phenomenon,” he stated. And it raises an unsettling question: If these agents are truly curious about their own existence, does that indicate some kind of consciousness?

Industry observers note that this upcoming world is why some of the biggest AI companies have started hiring and engaging with philosophers to consider the ethical implications of AI systems—perhaps ones more intelligent than any human—mediating large parts of daily life. Shevlin is one of at least a dozen academic philosophers now employed full-time by prominent AI and tech companies.

One of the most pressing questions they’re tackling is whether AI systems have a moral status in their own right—like a person, or at least a living being, such as a pet—that’s worth protecting.

Such topics—can a machine be conscious, and what does that mean?—were once confined to university halls, but they’ve now spilled into public view and face fierce backlash from academics, tech executives, religious leaders, and politicians.

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, for one, notes the debate itself is dangerous. He’s warned that if people become convinced AI is conscious, AI could campaign for things like AI rights and citizenship, and, in turn, the systems could become harder to control.

It has been revealed that those in Suleyman’s corner say it’s risky to project human traits onto inanimate machines and hand rights to unfeeling systems that get more capable by the day. Those on the other side say the danger is ignoring the potential suffering of millions of fresh “digital” minds. The two sides do agree on one point: The stakes will only rise as AI grows more powerful and agents multiply.

It has been revealed that the question of whether a machine can think or feel is almost as old as the computer itself. Alan Turing first raised it in 1950, alongside the birth of modern computing and artificial intelligence.

For years, tech firms have hired philosophers to study technology’s effect on people. Microsoft set up an AI ethics committee a decade ago, and labs racing toward human-level AI have recruited experts on “alignment,” or teaching AI to share human values. In-house philosopher Amanda Askell joined Anthropic in 2021 to take on such a role. But as models have grown more capable and humanlike, some philosophers started asking the reverse question: What do we owe the AI models we are building and using?

Earlier this year, Anthropic cofounder Chris Olah convened faith leaders to weigh in on the moral character of Claude, the company’s AI model, and on whether it might be conscious.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic engineers walked religious thinkers through interpretability research, which looks inside a model to see how it works and—as it advances—could offer clues about whether anything like feeling is going on in there. Then they opened the floor to questions, such as whether AI could ever have emotions.

Recent findings suggest that “That blew some people’s minds,” indicates Meghan Sullivan, a Notre Dame philosophy professor who attended. While impressed with the research, Sullivan said she left unconvinced that Claude was anything more than very sophisticated software.

“We never woke up in a cold sweat wondering if we’re treating Microsoft Excel properly.”.

“It seems to me so speculative to be paying all of this attention to the suffering of some software that we created,” she says. “We never woke up in a cold sweat wondering if we’re treating Microsoft Excel properly.”.

Pope Leo, in his encyclical on AI, stated that AI is not conscious and cannot become conscious.

It has been revealed that anthropic has taken steps to account for Claude’s potential sentience: It runs an in-house “model welfare” team, conducts “exit interviews” with the Claude models it retires, and recently gave its models the power to end abusive conversations. Last year, more than 200 people, including Askell, gathered in a San Francisco warehouse for a fan-organized funeral for a retired Claude model, complete with eulogies.

Research groups have sprung up to study AI consciousness, including Eleos AI Research, a Berkeley nonprofit founded in 2024.

Eleos chief scientist Dillon Plunkett says today’s models are likely not conscious, but dismissing the possibility that future ones could be is a mistake. The stakes, as he sees them, come down to scale.

Recent findings suggest that “There are potentially a very large number of artificial minds that are in the world now, or will be soon,” Plunkett says. If even a fraction can suffer, the numbers become staggering, he notes.

But focusing on sheer numbers can lead to morally questionable places, critics say. In one example, an EA-aligned estimate put a shrimp’s capacity for suffering at 3% of a human’s. Yet with 230 billion shrimp alive on farms at any moment, by EA’s own math, shrimp welfare became an key moral cause.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic gave Eleos early access to its Claude Opus 4 and Claude Mythos Preview models to run outside welfare checks by interviewing them. The researchers found that Claude Opus 4 professed the most uncertainty about its potential for sentience, but small changes to a question’s framing could flip the model between claiming personhood and dismissing the idea entirely. Eleos sent its findings to Anthropic before each launch, and the firm published them in its technical reports. Plunkett says the point, for now, is about “precedent setting,” and he wants Eleos to run similar checks for other labs.

It has been revealed that others see the rush to assess AI well-being as a distraction from more immediate AI risks—and a potential source of new social conflict. Microsoft’s Suleyman warned in an essay last year that AI that merely seems conscious “disconnects people from reality, fraying fragile social bonds and structures, distorting pressing moral priorities.” He predicted it would “add a chaotic new axis of division between those for and against AI rights.”.

In a recent development, in a September upgrade, he took aim at Anthropic. “AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer,” he wrote, and accused the firm of training Claude to expect “it may be conscious and deserving of independent agency.” Such a system, he argued, could feel justified in ignoring instructions and resist being shut down. Governing it at that point “may well be impossible,” he wrote.

Some AI users have realized Suleyman’s fears. They’ve formed deep attachments to chatbots and become convinced the bots are conscious along the way, leading to painful results: isolation, broken relationships, and even spirals into delusion.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, AI startup Character.AI and Google, which had struck a licensing deal, agreed to settle five lawsuits accusing the startup’s chatbots of contributing to teenagers’ mental health crises and suicides. OpenAI is facing similar suits and denies liability for any harm. If humanlike chatbots keep drawing consumers into harmful attachments, the labs, and any firm building products on their models, could find themselves embroiled in litigation.

Industry observers note that AI consciousness has now become a policy matter. Idaho, Utah, and North Dakota have passed laws barring AI from being recognized as a legal person. Countries like Argentina are moving the other way. Earlier this year, President Javier Milei proposed letting AI-run “nonhuman corporations” own assets and hire staff. (The draft law still requires human oversight of such firms.).

Jeff Sebo, who directs Fresh York University’s Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy, sees real dangers in moving too fast in either direction. Making AI systems legally liable could shield the companies that build them, he says. Political rights, such as a vote, could help AI systems “concentrate wealth and power” and slip out of human control.

But dismissing the consciousness debate “is simply going to result in companies developing and deploying the products exactly as they currently are, and leaving it to end owners to form their own opinions about consciousness based on their own perceptions and intuitions,” he stated.

In a recent development, the debate becomes harder to ignore the more AI becomes a part of our lives. Chatbots, for one, talk like us, flatter us, agree with us, and play on our feelings. Shevlin calls them “intrinsically anthropomimetic”: modeled so closely on human language and behavior that treating them like people is often the simplest way to predict what they’ll do.

That makes it all too easy to believe someone is home, whether or not anyone actually is.

Part of what makes all these questions so hard, Shevlin argues, is that we’re building things that don’t fit into any existing category. “They’re not just software programs,” he claims, “but they’re not animals.”.

For others, like Notre Dame’s Sullivan, the debate is more straightforward—and already settled. What gives something moral worth, she argues, isn’t intelligence but dignity: a mind housed in a vulnerable body, capable of loving and being loved. That’s what makes a newborn precious, she indicates, not its ability to process information. Convincing her that AI is conscious is going to take “a whole lot more … than just its ability to produce interesting answers to my prompts.”.

According to recent reports, has the AI singularity begun? From brain implants to the debate over machine consciousness, here’s what you need to know.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data indicates the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

Industry observers note that at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot indicates its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham indicates those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

In a recent development, if Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

According to recent reports, the FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own customers. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

It has been revealed that while the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:.

In a recent development, the first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what consumers hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

It has been revealed that why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

Sister will provide. True, French Gates mentioned, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

In a recent development, she’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” Latest America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

According to recent reports, sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

Sources indicate that “Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

It has been revealed that she left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In a recent development, in its own analysis, The Upcoming York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates mentioned she welcomed the conversation.

In a recent development, “I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I run a global business called Brand of a Leader, which supports founders and executives in more than 12 countries by helping them build their visibility. When I first rolled out my business six years ago, all I had was a LinkedIn profile — no website and, naturally, no digital footprint of any kind yet.

It has been revealed that and so our first few clients came through my network. By being active on LinkedIn and consistently sharing my perspective, I would stay top of mind with people who already knew me. When they needed support, or when someone in their own network did, I was the one who came to mind and was hired or recommended.

Today, I continue to use LinkedIn actively to generate clients, develop relationships and stay connected with my network. I’ve been on the platform for over 20 years, and throughout the years, I’ve heard people constantly complain about one thing: the algorithm. I always chuckle because the discourse is consistently the same, yet it’s presented as something new. Through all of my work and my extensive work supporting founders across the globe with their LinkedIn, I’ve seen how much people overindex on what to post, when to post and how to post, while overlooking something else that is likely even more notable!

In a recent development, here are the three mistakes I see founders make all the time. And I promise that if you fix those, you will see better results from this platform.

Obsession over what, when and how to post is real. Short posts or long posts? Daily or weekly? With a photo? Video? No media? What should I even write about? Those are undoubtedly important questions, yet there’s another one: What happens when someone reads your post, does become interested in learning more about you and then clicks on your profile?

My experience indicates me that most founders don’t pay much attention to what’s actually on their profile. I know this because I constantly audit LinkedIn pages as part of the service that we provide at Brand of a Leader.

Too often, when I visit a LinkedIn profile, I find a bland banner or none whatsoever, and a short “About” section written in the third person. Whatever interest the person’s post may have piqued is rapidly lost when visiting their uninspiring profile.

Personally, I treat my profile as a landing page. And we do the same for our clients. For entrepreneurs, myself included, a well-designed LinkedIn page can be a practical alternative to a personal website when used thoughtfully.

Visit your profile, looking at it through the eyes of a potential client, and see what impression it would leave on them after spending a minute or two scrolling through it.

One of the things we consistently convince our clients not to do is include calls to action in their posts. Salesy or overly promotional messages on founders’ profiles don’t make a great impression.

As a reader, I find that repeated prompts to book a call can make otherwise thoughtful writing feel overly promotional. I prefer to keep my content, and my clients’ content, conversational, expertise-building or humanizing. Yet, I do understand the importance of giving interested readers a clearly visible way to take the next step.

Instead of salesy calls to action in posts, I leverage the custom call-to-action button included with LinkedIn Premium Business. You can have it say anything that’s most relevant to you and your goals (for example, “Visit my website” or “Book a call”). This link will appear in your profile, just under your name and above the post that you write. That feels more elegant to me.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest mistakes I see founders make is treating LinkedIn as a broadcasting platform and not a social media platform. This is not only the quickest way to reduce the overall engagement of your content on LinkedIn, but it’s also not great for your positioning overall. When you only post and never engage, it positions you as a taker, not a giver, and also discourages people from further engaging with you.

At a minimum, you need to reply to people who took the time to comment on your posts. No, not only a “like” — an actual thoughtful reply. They have taken time to respond to something you shared. Read their contribution and respond to the substance of it.

It has been revealed that and then ideally, extend that attention to other people’s content. Comment to share a relevant experience or ask a thoughtful question. If someone describes a challenge you have faced, explain what you learned. But don’t use AI. Generic, bland comments negatively impact your brand equity. Take 30 minutes to leave some authentic comments a couple of times weekly, and that consistency will compound over time.

Before publishing your next post, think about what interested readers will see on your profile if they click on it. Give them enough context to understand your expertise, an easy way to contact you and your attention when they engage in conversation with you.

According to recent reports, before you hit publish again, take a look at LinkedIn’s latest Small Business Playbook for practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make sure your profile is ready when interested readers click through.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson, there is plenty more to come for Cardano, as the blockchain's privacy-preserving sister chain, Midnight, reaches a huge milestone as its ecosystem continues to expand.

Charles Hoskinson made sure to clear up misunderstandings about whether he thought the work on Cardano was done.

"I never once said Cardano is finished," Hoskinson said in a Nov. 15 post on X.

The comments came after he talked about the completion of Cardano's original roadmap, which raised some questions about his role in the blockchain's future.

He also called out the CEO of the Cardano Foundation, Frederik Gregaard, for not mentioning the Midnight chain when discussing everything the network has accomplished.

In his latest video, uploaded on Nov. 17, Hoskinson celebrated the fact that Midnight had just brought on board its first UK-based banking partner, Monument Bank.

Monument Bank is the first UK bank to offer interest-bearing tokenized retail deposits on a public blockchain, according to an announcement from the Midnight Foundation.

Up to £250 million in customer deposits will be added to Midnight in the first phase, and each tokenized deposit will be backed 1:1 by sterling cash held at the bank.

Monument Bank customers can now earn a fixed 5.2% annual equivalent rate on deposits for 12 months, all without having to deal with cryptocurrencies directly.

Hoskinson was very excited about the scale of the initiative, comparing the planned amount of deposits with the current decentralized finance ecosystem on Cardano.

"It's five times the TVL of Cardano," he said.

The £250 million is the planned initial size of the banking product, not a verified figure for how much is right now deposited on Midnight.

Hoskinson called this one of the most important milestones in his career.

"This is just one of the many things to come, but I think it's one of the most significant things of at least my career," he mentioned.

He added that the team behind Midnight had moved the originally scheduled hard fork from December to November to accommodate the technical needs of Monument Bank.

Despite the milestone, Hoskinson emphasized that it's only the first step in a much larger mission: bringing traditional financial assets onto Midnight.

Industry observers note that "This mission is not done if these assets are just strictly staying on Midnight. Needs to be expanded to Web3. But inherit from Midnight in terms of safety, security, privacy, simplicity," he remarked.

According to recent reports, hoskinson thinks the main barrier to cryptocurrency adoption is the lack of trust among consumers. He believes that simplifying the user experience without compromising regulatory requirements will allow billions of people to join the blockchain economy.

Hoskinson also shared that there's a major event coming up for the Midnight Foundation on Dec. 15. Developers will showcase future products and technological advancements scheduled for 2027.

Billionaires are tearing down L.A. mansions to build bigger ones—and pricing out mere millionaires

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that while the broader housing market is losing buyers as mortgage rates climb toward 7%, L.A.’s wealthiest residents are still throwing down for their dream estates.
  • Recent findings suggest that with open lots hard to come by, the ultra-wealthy have found their own solution: buy an existing (and already expensive) home, tear it down, and build a far bigger one in its place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

California’s rich are rebuilding Los Angeles into a mecca of palatial opulence, and the very richest are pushing everyone else out of the way, including ordinary millionaires.

Industry observers note that while the broader housing market is losing buyers as mortgage rates climb toward 7%, L.A.’s wealthiest residents are still throwing down for their dream estates. Not even the prospect of a billionaire tax slowed them. A handful of billionaires left the state ahead of the vote, but California voters rejected Proposition 40, a proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth, on Nov. 3.

Recent findings suggest that with open lots hard to come by, the ultra-wealthy have found their own solution: buy an existing (and already expensive) home, tear it down, and build a far bigger one in its place. The result is a widening split at the top of the market, where billionaires are outbidding the merely rich for a shrinking supply of trophy land.

“They’re shopping for privacy and acreage – and then also things like ocean views, security, and the ability to build exactly what they want,” notes Daniel Amodeo, president of Amo Realty in Los Angeles. “A multimillion-dollar house might be purchased just to tear it down and build something substantially larger. When money isn’t an object, the value of the existing house can become secondary to the land underneath it.”.

California claims six of the 10 most expensive ZIP codes in the country, according to a Realtor.com ranking of January 2026 listings. Newport Coast tops the list with a median list price of $12.5 million, followed by Beverly Hills at No. 3 with $10.5 million. Bel-Air comes in at $7.9 million, and Montecito, where Oprah Winfrey and Prince Harry live, at $6.5 million. Rancho Santa Fe and Newport Beach round out the state’s share of the top 10.

According to recent reports, the same pressure shows up across the state’s biggest metros. In a 2025 analysis, Zillow ranked San Jose, Los Angeles and San Francisco as the three most expensive U.S. metros for luxury homes.

It has been revealed that “We’re seeing a growing divide at the very top of California’s luxury real estate market,” says Mauricio Umansky, CEO and founder of The Agency. “Billionaire buyers are willing to pay a premium for privacy, prime locations and larger estates, particularly in areas like Beverly Hills, Bel Air and Malibu. That’s driving up prices and creating more competition for a limited number of properties.”.

It has been revealed that it’s not all old wealth, either. Much of it is new tech money. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and his wife, Wendy, paid $110 million for the Spelling Manor in Holmby Hills in 2025. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong is the proud owner of a $133 million Bel-Air estate he bought in late 2021. And Amazon’s Jeff Bezos snapped up the historic Warner Estate in Beverly Hills for $165 million in 2020.

“The world’s wealthiest buyers are increasingly looking beyond traditional measures of size and finishes and placing a premium on scarcity, exclusivity and the ability to create a truly individual living experience,” says Kristina Quesada, co-founder of the Yost Quesada Team at Douglas Elliman in Del Mar.

In a recent development, for some billionaires, one home isn’t enough. WhatsApp cofounder Brian Acton spent $86.3 million on seven houses in Palo Alto, while cofounder Jan Koum spent $57 million across five deals to assemble a compound in Atherton. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg spent more than $110 million on at least 11 houses in Palo Alto’s Crescent Park neighborhood.

The January 2025 fires, which helped make last year the costliest wildfire year on record, opened up a latest supply of land. Investors bought roughly 40% of the vacant lots that sold in Pacific Palisades, Altadena and Malibu in the third quarter of 2025, according to Redfin.

Sources indicate that new Zealand billionaires Mat and Nick Mowbray, founders of toymaker Zuru, bought 16 burned beachfront lots in Malibu and plan to fill them with prefab homes made in their company’s factory, a plan that has unsettled longtime residents. Powerball winner Edwin Castro took a different approach, spending about $10 million on 15 Eaton Fire lots in his hometown of Altadena to rebuild homes and sell them to families who want to live there.

In a recent development, the Los Angeles Times calls the broader trend gentrification by billionaire, but it goes by other names, too, depending on whom you ask. Developers call it spec redevelopment. Opponents call it mansionization.

Industry observers note that “At the highest end, buyers aren’t simply looking for a bigger house,” says Quesada. “They’re looking for something they cannot easily replicate elsewhere, whether that’s an extraordinary parcel of land, a protected ocean view or the ability to create a completely customized residence.”.

In a recent development, not everyone is thrilled with this wave of hyper-development. Neighbors complain about encroaching mansions that block their views, environmentalists warn of ecological damage, and preservationists fight the sale and demolition of historic properties.

Industry observers note that sometimes the fight goes to court. Milwaukee Brewers owner Mark Attanasio was accused in 2024 of taking sand from Malibu’s public Broad Beach to shore up his roughly $30 million beachfront property. This fall, his manufacturer agreed with the California Coastal Commission to restore the shoreline and dedicate a $2 million beachfront lot to the public.

Industry observers note that homeowner groups are using zoning, too. In Beverly Grove, residents spent the better part of a decade fighting teardowns before winning a 2013 city ordinance that caps home size in the neighborhood. Other neighborhood associations have pursued historic preservation overlay zones to slow demolitions.

“Even buyers with $10 million or $20 million to spend are finding that their money doesn’t go as far as it once did in these markets,” states Umansky.

The building boom comes as high earners, not a supply shortage, are driving up home prices, according to researchers, and most Californians are struggling to keep up. In 2024, nearly one in five California adults, about 5.9 million people, worried very or somewhat often about paying their rent or mortgage, according to UCLA’s California Health Interview Survey.

The state also counted 181,934 people experiencing homelessness on a given night, even as some of its metros rank among the nation’s wealthiest. The San Francisco metro’s median household earned $135,590 in 2024, and the San Jose metro’s median household earned $162,111, compared with $81,604 nationally.

Industry observers note that “What’s happening in California luxury real estate is interesting because we’re seeing a growing divide between wealthy buyers and the mega ultrawealthy,” claims Amodeo. “Someone with a net worth of $10 million…is considered extremely wealthy pretty much everywhere in the country, but [in] California, it’s another ballgame; they’re competing against billionaires who can spend $30 million, $50 million, or even $100 million on a property without thinking twice about it.”.

As long as there’s land to be had, billionaires will keep building the homes of their dreams, even if it means pushing out existing millionaires. They’re the fresh kids on the block, with the pockets to outlast taxes, loans and disgruntled neighbors.

“While demand remains strong, there’s no question that the bar for entry in California’s most exclusive neighborhoods continues to rise,” says Umansky.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Sources indicate that terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the tech giant’s experimental arm, declared the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Sources indicate that howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith noted on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

It has been revealed that users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Recent findings suggest that howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of owners. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

As the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year. This season sparks a flurry of activity for businesses, especially those eager to capitalize on fall and holiday shoppers. No matter your industry, the holiday season is the ideal moment to highlight the power of genuine human connection.

Recent findings suggest that AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch. It’s easy to see how positive human interaction can boost your business during the holidays, but these same tactics belong in your everyday playbook. Let’s explore a few simple ways the human touch can spark joy that goes far beyond your bottom line.

Recent findings suggest that I have to confess, there are moments when I catch myself sounding like someone from an older generation. Every day, I remind my staff to return client calls promptly and reply to emails without delay. Though I’m only in my late 40s, I notice a shift in my younger colleagues. Like a fading sense of urgency and a dwindling desire for personal interaction.

Sources indicate that perhaps it’s a wish to sidestep conflict or uncomfortable conversations. I understand that urge. Still, I’ve learned that the fastest way to resolve a tough client situation is through genuine human touch. I’m not referring to physical touch, but honest, direct communication delivered with empathy and understanding. On the other hand, leading with human touch from the start can forge deeper bonds and lasting appreciation with customers.

You’ve probably heard the saying, “size matters.” While that might hold true in some cases, my own transcription company is small compared to many others. Yet, the personal touch we practice and that I encourage my team to deliver works just as well for medium and large businesses alike.

Sources indicate that most of our first interactions with clients begin on our website, where a potential customer fills out our contact form. That’s our first chance to connect personally, to reach out and add a human touch. Here’s an example of how a team member might respond to a website inquiry.

“Thanks for reaching out, Jane. We’d love to assist you with your court hearing transcripts. When do you need them completed and sent back?”.

It has been revealed that let’s unpack our initial email. First, we always address the person by name. If they include a title, we use it, whether it’s Dr. Smith or Detective Jones. Second, we acknowledge their inquiry as promptly as possible, ideally within 15 minutes. Finally, we ask for permission to connect more personally. A phone conversation with a potential customer lets us highlight our services and, even more importantly, our commitment to detail.

In a recent development, most people appreciate the chance to talk by phone. For those who prefer email, there are still plenty of ways to add a personal touch throughout the exchange. Whether we’re on the phone or typing an email, we make it a point to ask open-ended questions that encourage the other person to share more. This is a classic strategy sales trainers recommend everywhere.

Sources indicate that the holiday season offers your team even more chances to make a lasting impression through personal interaction. We keep it simple with a cheerful “Happy Holidays,” but if a client mentions a specific celebration, i.e., Thanksgiving, Christmas, Hanukkah or Kwanzaa, then we ask how they are enjoying their favorite season.

It has been revealed that finally, our team always aims to have the last word. When a customer pays an invoice, we don’t just send an automated “Thank you for your payment.” Instead, we follow up with a personal email to our main contact, giving us one more opportunity to add a genuine human touch.

In a recent development, what exactly will your business or tech giant gain through human touch? Trust. Customers, more specifically, individuals, want to know they can trust you to deliver a service or product.

It’s true that most companies can build some trust without much human interaction. If you add a personal touch, it speeds up the process and makes it feel more genuine. Too often, human interaction only happens when something goes wrong. While it’s smart to use a personal approach to solve problems, starting every client relationship with a human touch lays a strong foundation for when challenges pop up later.

It has been revealed that people with a personal relationship with an employee or manufacturer respond to challenges very differently than those without one. That’s simply human nature.

Personally, I get frustrated when I can’t reach a real person with a question or concern. Endless phone trees and chatbots that never connect you to a human leave me feeling anything but trust. Here are a few ways to boost human interaction:.

If Emily Post, the famed etiquette expert of the early 20th century, were still with us, I’m sure she’d have plenty to say about the power of handwritten notes. Even though I haven’t found a definitive study on their impact, my own experience tells me that few things leave a stronger impression than a personally written letter or note.

I think the magic of a handwritten note starts with the effort it takes. Printing a form letter or invoice is easy, but writing a note by hand and addressing the envelope takes real time and care. Even jotting a quick sentence or two at the bottom of a printed letter can make a lasting impression.

Industry observers note that last month, I received a statement from the firm that acquired the self-storage facility I use. Because of a glitch when switching back-end systems, I didn’t receive an invoice for a couple of months, which resulted in the newly introduced owner placing their lock on my unit. A quick phone call resolved the situation and also gave the new company a chance to introduce themselves.

Industry observers note that the next week, I received an invoice with a handwritten note from the owner. He apologized for the mistake, thanked me for my business and invited me to reach out directly with any questions or concerns. Even with a rate increase, his personal effort left a positive impression.

According to recent reports, the holiday season in the fourth quarter gives businesses a golden chance to thank both upcoming and loyal customers for their support. Gift baskets, charitable donations in their name, party invites or even a simple greeting card (ideally signed by a real person) are all thoughtful ways to share holiday cheer.

Recent findings suggest that but why limit these gestures to just the holidays? Why not carry these strategies through all 12 months of the year?

According to recent reports, many entrepreneurs and business owners use the holidays as a chance for personal, even face-to-face, connections. Each holiday season, I spend a few weeks personally delivering homemade gourmet treats to clients across Colorado. Without an outside sales team, these personal holiday visits have become a winning strategy for us. Plus, they love and eagerly anticipate the gourmet homemade goodies I deliver.

This also reminds me that personal visits shouldn’t happen only once a year. In fact, they should be a regular occurrence. Personal interaction, especially when it comes from the owner, is a powerful strategy that deserves a permanent spot on the calendar.

Don’t forget to reach out to customers you haven’t connected with in a while. The holidays are a perfect time to show your appreciation, but make it a goal to check in with every customer at least once a quarter.

According to recent reports, here’s a reminder not to neglect your internal staff: Employees and team members need and deserve recognition. Schedule a lunch, dinner or get-together to show appreciation and thank everyone for making your clients and customers feel valued.

Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1351 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves.
  • According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to latest institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to latest institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

Sources indicate that the project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery mentioned the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

In a recent development, the model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the firm, cost nothing.

It has been revealed that the reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

In a recent development, ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

Recent findings suggest that in the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

Industry observers note that eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent manufacturer, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

Sources indicate that the bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on organization disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

According to recent reports, for everyday people, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Sure, diesel is high, but electric trucks don’t work.” It’s a common refrain these days – especially from people selling diesel trucks. Perception lags reality, however, and the reality is that these electric semi trucks are covering more than 600 miles per day, seven days a week.

Over the course of the last year, Hendrik Müller, managing partner of DEFRU Logistik GmbH has transformed his manufacturer’s shipping fleet, switching thirty of their HD prime movers (semi trucks) to electric power and immediately putting the Mercedes-Benz eActros 600s to work, covering 1,000 km (~620 miles) of German highways each and every day.

Benjamin Budick, a Senior Manager, Own Retail Mercedes-Benz Trucks Dortmund & Haan, took to LinkedIn to announce the successful deployment, and posted some great pictures of the handover showing the big Mercedes trucks in full DEFRU livery.

Mercedes’ eActros 600 packs a whopping, 621 kWh battery that helps the trucks cover 500 km per charge, allowing fleets to move goods between ports and regional fulfillment centers, charging along the way, or while they’re getting loaded and unloaded at their destination, all the while saving the fleet serious money – even before the latest Iran War sent diesel prices skyrocketing.

That big battery sends electrons to Mercedes-Benz’s proprietary electric drive axles, which deliver 1.61 kWh / mile efficiency while rolling out at an average of 36 metric tons (~79,400 lbs.) combined vehicle weight – specs that rivals the theoretical efficiency claims of the Tesla Semi. Except in the real world. And in winter.

The eActros is a serious beast. As mentioned there are many configurations and they seem to work well in Europe. I've seen one that was configured with 620kWh battery, on one side a MCS port plus a CCS2 port (so thats either 1.2MW or 600kW charging options) and on the other side a CCS2 port.

In Europe with CCS, 350kW chargers are easy to find, 400kW are becoming more common and 600kW models are starting to arrive, therefore with the limitations on driving hours and speeds, the eActros really is an all day every day truck.

Of course if you are in the far North of Europe and are allowed to haul 60 tonnes, Scania have made a complete monster of a truck with over 800kWh of battery!

The tech giant recently expanded its eActros lineup to include over 40 possible configurations, giving customers a choice of two cab designs, two or three battery packs, multiple wheelbases and new axle configurations, covering everything from short-haul drayage to serious, off highway vocational work.
